name: The Sherman household — a documented dressmaker, unplaced in the town
head: sherman_h

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 3 December 1834, column 21, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-12-03 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1834-12-03.

lives_at.note: Not attested. NOTHING IS BEING WITHHELD HERE: no source reached says where this person lived, and 52 households in this dataset were already in that position before this one was written.

works_at.note: Not attested as a structure this project models. The trade is documented; the premises are not one of the committed records.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1834-12-03, at the Democrat of 3 December 1834, column 21, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

persons.name: Mrs. H. Sherman

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as dress maker, milliner, at the Democrat of 3 December 1834, column 21. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `dressmaker`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name ''RS. H. SHERMAN,' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 3 December 1834, column 21. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `dressmaker` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Sherman, Howard | Letter. | December 29, 1852. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0812, printed page 200), admitted 1852-12-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Sherman' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins H. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

resident_research.evidence_for: No reliable record found in the reviewed web, institutional-history, digitized-book, newspaper-index and genealogy-finding-aid searches could be tied to this 1835 Chicago person without relying on the name alone.
resident_research.notes: No candidate fact is asserted unless a source bridges the candidate to the 1835 Chicago record by more than name similarity.
resident_research.summary: Nothing reviewed in this pass corroborates Mrs. H. Sherman from outside the record already held: the fergus chicago directory 1843, norris directory 1844 agreement is a surname-only refusal; the papers carry the name 1834-12-03 as dressmaker.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

merge_ruling.for_merge: One letter dropped from a nine-letter surname, the initial H on both, and the Sherman card is documented with a trade: 'MRS. H. SHERMAN' the dressmaker, in the Democrat of 3 December 1834 (#c021) and the 1840 census at 212:12. 'Shearman' is set nowhere in the deposited corpus.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE HONORIFIC FIXES A DIFFERENT PERSON, AND THE SECOND INITIAL IS UNMATCHED. The Sherman reading is 'Mrs. H. Sherman' — a married woman, named by her husband's initial in the form the period used — while the letter-list reading is 'H. C. Shearman', a man's two initials, on the return of 28 January 1834 (#c001). A fold would put a correspondent's two initials onto a dressmaker's card and lose the Mrs. that is the only thing either source says about who she is. C9's first condition fails on the C and on the honorific together. SHERMAN IS HEAVILY POPULATED HERE — sherman_h, sherman_rebecca, sherman_silas_w, sherman_william_george, and 482 settings in the corpus — and T-0480 closed the Shearman card no_corroboration_yet after searching the 1839 and 1843 directories. D10.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Mrs. H. Sherman as a dressmaker at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.
